questions.prompt: Why does `Buffer(std::size_t n) : cap(n), data(new int[cap]) {}` exhibit undefined behavior?
options: `new int[cap]` cannot appear inside a member initializer list.
`std::size_t` cannot be converted inside an initializer list.
`data` is declared before `cap`, so `data` initializes first and reads an uninitialized `cap`.
Member initializer lists evaluate strictly right-to-left.
questions.explanation: Under `[class.base.init]/13`, non-static data members always initialize in declaration order inside the class body (`data`, then `cap`), ignoring the order written in the colon initializer list. `data(new int[cap])` reads indeterminate `cap` before `cap(n)` runs.

questions.prompt: When constructing a `std::string` member `name_` from a parameter, why should you prefer `: name_(std::move(s))` over `name_ = std::move(s);` in the constructor body?
options: The member initializer constructs `name_` once in place instead of default-constructing it first and then move-assigning.
Assignment inside a constructor body is forbidden for standard library types.
`std::move` only works inside member initializer lists.
Member initializers skip calling `~std::string()` at destruction.
questions.explanation: Every member not named in the mem-initializer list is initialized before entering the constructor body (`[class.base.init]/9`), so assigning inside `{ ... }` performs default construction followed by assignment. Mem-initializers construct once directly and are mandatory for `const`, reference, and non-default-constructible members.

questions.prompt: Given `Base::Base()` calling `virtual const char* kind() const`, what does `Derived d;` cause `Base::Base()` to observe when `Derived` overrides `kind()`?
options: "Derived", because the vptr already points to `Derived`'s vtable.
Undefined behavior whenever any virtual function is called from a constructor.
Compile error: virtual functions cannot be called inside constructors.
"Base", because during `Base::Base()` the dynamic type of the object is `Base`.
questions.explanation: Under `[class.cdtor]/4`, while a base constructor or destructor is executing, the object's dynamic type is that base class (`Base`), not the still-uninitialized `Derived` class. Virtual dispatch resolves to `Base::kind()`.

questions.prompt: In a virtual-inheritance diamond `struct Derived : Left, Right`, where `Left() : VBase(1)` and `Right() : VBase(2)` and `Derived() : Left(), Right()` omits `VBase`, how is `VBase` initialized?
options: `VBase(1)` runs via `Left`, and `Right`'s `VBase(2)` is skipped.
`Derived` acts as the most-derived class and default-initializes `VBase(0)`, ignoring both `Left` and `Right`'s `VBase` initializers.
Compile error: `Derived` must explicitly repeat `VBase(1)` or `VBase(2)`.
`VBase` is constructed twice—once with `1` and once with `2`.
questions.explanation: `[class.base.init]/7` specifies that virtual base classes are initialized solely by the most-derived class (`Derived`), ignoring `VBase(...)` mem-initializers in intermediate bases `Left` and `Right`. Because `Derived` omitted `VBase`, `VBase` is default-initialized with `0`.

questions.prompt: If a delegating constructor finishes calling its target constructor and then throws inside its own compound body `{ ... }`, does `~Widget()` execute?
options: No; `~Widget()` never executes if any constructor throws.
Only if `Widget(int)` was marked `noexcept`.
Yes; once the target constructor completes, the object's lifetime has begun so `~Widget()` runs during unwinding.
Undefined behavior unless caught inside a function-try-block.
questions.explanation: Unlike a non-delegating constructor (where throwing destroys only constructed subobjects), `[except.ctor]/3` states that an object whose constructor delegates is considered fully constructed once the target constructor returns normally. Therefore throwing in the delegating body invokes `~Widget()`.

questions.prompt: Why does `Point p{1, 2};` fail to compile in C++20 and C++23 when `Point` declares `Point() = default;`?
options: `= default` makes `Point` trivial rather than initializable with braces.
In C++20+, any user-declared constructor—even `= default` or `= delete`—disqualifies a class from being an aggregate.
Aggregate initialization only works when all members have default member initializers.
`Point()` must be declared `constexpr` to support `{1, 2}`.
questions.explanation: Prior to C++20, defaulted or deleted constructors did not prevent a class from being an aggregate. C++20 (`[dcl.init.aggr]/1`) changed the definition so *any* user-declared or inherited constructor makes the class a non-aggregate, leaving `Point p{1, 2}` with no matching two-argument constructor.
